title: India Records Warmest August Since 1901 as Monsoon Deficit Hits 14%
excerpt: El Niño-driven heat and feeble rainfall leave nearly half of India’s districts parched, with September offering little relief for crops and reservoirs.
body:
• India recorded its warmest August since 1901, with a mean temperature of 28.01°C — 0.67°C above the long-period average — as El Niño strengthens across the Pacific.
  • August rainfall fell 16.3% short of normal, pushing the cumulative monsoon deficit to 14% and leaving 47% of India’s 741 districts under deficient rains.
  • The India Meteorological Department forecasts below-normal rainfall in September, raising concerns over kharif crop yields, reservoir levels, and food inflation.
  • Only Odisha received excess rain, thanks to back-to-back low-pressure systems in the Bay of Bengal, while Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, and several other states remain rain-starved.

India has recorded its hottest August in 125 years, capping a punishing monsoon season that is deepening worries over food security, water reserves, and the rural economy.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) confirmed on Monday that August 2026 registered a mean temperature of 28.01°C, nearly 0.67°C above the long-period average. Night temperatures were also the highest on record for August since observations began in 1901, according to IMD chief Dr. Mrutyunjay Mohapatra.

A Season of Deficits

The heat was driven in large part by feeble monsoon rainfall. August ended with a precipitation shortfall of 16.3%, with actual rainfall well below the normal of 254.9 mm. That follows a staggering 35% deficit in June, only partially offset by near-normal rains in July. The cumulative seasonal deficit from June through August now stands at 14%.

"“We had forecast the seasonal rainfall to be less than 90% of the long-period average, with +/-4%, and we stand by that,” Mohapatra said."

Of the 741 districts assessed by the IMD, 312 — or 42% — received below-normal rainfall, while 38 districts reported large deficient conditions. States including Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Bihar, and several northeastern states remain in deficit.

“This is a weak monsoon year. When El Niño forms, it causes significant compression of air over the Indian region, leading to warmer air and higher temperatures.”
— Dr. Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, IMD Director General

El Niño and the MJO

Mohapatra attributed the shortfall to two factors: a strengthening El Niño — the warming of sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean — and an unfavorable phase of the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), which suppressed convection over the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea.

The MJO, a large-scale atmospheric disturbance that moves eastward on a 30-to-60-day cycle, can enhance or diminish monsoon rainfall depending on its phase. July’s near-normal rains coincided with a favorable MJO phase, but that window closed by August.

Two break conditions in August — from the 5th through the 16th and from the 27th through the 31st — pushed the monsoon trough north of its normal position, cutting off rainfall across the Indo-Gangetic plains. Six low-pressure systems formed in the Bay of Bengal during the month, above the normal of 5.3, but they remained active for 26 days versus the usual 16.3, disproportionately benefiting the east coast. Odisha was the only state to receive excess rainfall.

September Outlook Offers Little Relief

The IMD forecast for September — the final month of the monsoon season — holds more bad news. Monthly rainfall is expected to be below normal, less than 91% of the long-period average, as El Niño conditions strengthen further. The agency had earlier predicted below-normal seasonal rainfall and reiterated its forecast. “We had forecast the seasonal rainfall to be less than 90% of the long-period average, with +/-4%, and we stand by that,” Mohapatra said.

Crop and Water Concerns

The deficit threatens India’s kharif crop season. Sowing of summer crops including rice, soybeans, and pulses is nearly complete but about 2% below last year’s acreage. With September rains expected to fall short, farmers face higher irrigation costs for standing crops at a time when reservoir levels are declining.

The monsoon delivers nearly 70% of the rain the $3-trillion economy needs to water farms and replenish aquifers. A shortfall of this magnitude could boost food prices and overall inflation, adding pressure on a government already grappling with rising costs.

What’s Next

Some areas of northwest, northeast, east-central, and southeast peninsular India may see normal to above-normal rainfall in September, but that is unlikely to compensate for the broader deficit. Climate scientists note that El Niño events have historically been associated with weaker monsoons and elevated temperatures in India — and the current event is expected to gain further strength through the end of the year.
